newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico cement firms seen weathering U.S. tariff.
newsitem.headline: Mexico cement firms seen weathering U.S. tariff.

text.p: Mexican cement firms will not be badly hurt by a recent decision by a binational panel to uphold a U.S. anti-dumping tariff on Mexican cement, analysts said.

Despite predictions by Mexico's Commerce Minister Herminio Blance recently that the 1990 U.S. Commerce Department ruling would be overturned by the panel, Mexican cement companies and most analysts expected the duty to stay on the books.
"It was an expected decision and should not affect the outlook for Mexico's cement industry," said Gordon Lee, a cement analyst at Deutche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.

The binational panel -- made up of three U.S. representatives and two Mexicans -- decided last Friday that a duty of 61.85 percent on Mexican gray portland and clinker cement did not break U.S. trade laws.
Cemex, the world's third largest cement company in terms of installed capacity, was the company most interested in having the tariff revoked.
Since the tariff was applied in 1990, Cemex has shipped most of its exports to the U.S. market from Spain and Venezuela to get around the duty -- a costly move considering the weight of cement.

But Cemex has limited its exposure to the tariff by boosting production in its U.S. units in Texas, Arizona and California. It has also shifted exports toward Asia and Latin America from the U.S. market.
During 1996, the company expects to export just 30-35 percent of its production to the U.S. market, compared to about 40 percent during 1995.
"The panel's decision to keep the tariff does not affect Cemex in the least. Had they lifted the tariff then Cemex would have benefitted," said Paul Rodriguez, an analyst at Caspian Research.

Grupo Cementos Chihuahua (GCC), another player in the U.S. market with operations in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, plans to export about 400,000 tonnes to the United States this year, about 28 percent of its total production.
"GCC is located so close to the U.S. border, that its transport costs are low and it can still deliver a price of about $71-$72 per tonne, which is competitive," another analyst said.
Apasco, a unit of Switzerland's Holderbank and Mexico's second biggest cement firm, does not export to the U.S. market.
Analysts said they were still hopeful the duty would be scrapped in the coming years.
"I think they'll get rid of it, but not in 1996 with an election coming up. Maybe in 1997 we'll see something different," Lee said.
